utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, everybody, and good afternoon to you, Madam Registrar. If you could call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, madam. For the record, all the accused are here. From the Defence teams, I notice the absence of Mr. Haynes, Mr. Bourgon, and Mr. Ostojic. The Prosecution is represented by Mr. McCloskey and Mr. Vanderpuye. The witness is already in the courtroom. So good afternoon to you, Mr. Savcic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And we are going to continue with your testimony which we started yesterday. I just wish to remind you of two things; namely, that you are testifying with the solemn declaration that you made yesterday still in force, and, secondly, I want you to remember all the time what I told you yesterday about your right to ask to be exempted from answering certain questions. Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon to you. Good afternoon, Your Honours, good afternoon to counsel. Good afternoon, Mr. Savcic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yesterday when we left off I was asking you about the function of the 65th Protection Regiment, and you had explained the role of the Military Police Battalion in very general terms. Was the regiment also engaged in defensive as well as offensive deployments?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, Mr. Vanderpuye, if you just allow me to expand the answer I started giving yesterday about the military police and its jurisdiction, its purview.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Members of military police units exercised their duties in the spirit of the rules governing the military police and doing the service of the military police. That service includes providing security, thus members of the military police secure command posts, military leaders, stationary and in movement, documents, especially those that are marked "Confidential." They secure assets of military equipment, et cetera. Another duty of the military police is patrol duty. The military police patrol, when the situation requires that, usually with the aim of controlling the military regiment. The third duty is pursuit and search, such as searching for military conscripts who have gone absent without official leave or people who are on the run. Another of their duties is escort, such as escorting prisoners who were remanded in custody by military courts, et cetera. Another duty is military traffic control. I don't think that needs explanation. And yet another duty is crime prevention. These are the duties that military police service encompasses and that I did not have time to enumerate yesterday. And to answer the question you just asked, units of the Protection Regiment are used in keeping with the rules that govern them, in keeping with orders of their superior command, but they can also be used in defensive and offensive actions when the situation and the orders require them to be thus engaged.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much for that. Now, during July 1995, I just want to get into, very generally, the structure of the regiment, who was your deputy commander?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to establishment, it was the deputy commander of the regiment, Colonel Jovo Jazic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And what was his responsibility, just generally?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was chief of Staff, and he leads the work of the Staff. That includes the chief of the Operations and Training, chief of Personnel and Reinforcement, chief of Communications, and the Office of General Affairs. You see, it's a bit different on regiment level than at brigade level, but it doesn't have various branches, engineering, artillery, et cetera, and there are no other assistants, so the staff is narrower than is the case at brigade level. He leads the work of these organs, of these bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And as your deputy chief of Staff, is he entitled to sign orders on your behalf?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my absence, yes. That's why he is my deputy. I have to emphasise before this Court that from 12 October 1994 to 23rd June 1995, I was absent from the unit for hospital treatment that resulted from a serious wound. In that case, the commander of the regiment was in the hands of Deputy Commander Lieutenant-Colonel Jazic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If you can briefly outline what the various structures in the regiment were at that time in July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the units of the regiment?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: The units of the regiment and their commanders, if you can recall their names.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember. If you allow me, I just want to finish with the command of the regiment. We spoke about the staff, and in addition to that, I had an Assistant for Morale, Religious and Legal affairs and an Assistant for Logistics. The establishment envisaged that I should also have an assistant for Intelligence and Security, but due to a shortage in personnel, that vacancy wasn't filled, so I didn't have that assistant. Now, for command, as far as units are concerned in 1995, the regiment had the following units: A Motorised Battalion, a battalion of military police, a sabotage detachment, an artillery rocket battalion of antiaircraft defence, a tank company, a logistical company, and a transport company. That was the structure of the Protection Regiment. And I believe I also had a mortar company that I didn't mention. I have to stress that this structure of the regiment resulted from our practical needs. Initially, the regiment was not structured this way. Initially, it consisted of a battalion of military police, a sabotage detachment, an artillery/rocket battalion, a logistical company, a transport company, and on paper we had a scouting company and a radio reconnaissance company that did not actually exist. The Motorised Battalion, the tank company, and mixed mortar company or battery formed part of the structure.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Savcic. Do you recall the names, in particular, of the members of your Command?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the Command, I said the chief of Staff was simultaneously the Deputy Commander, he was Lieutenant-Colonel Jazic Jovo. The chief of training and operations was Vojislav Jarovic, then major. My assistant for morale, religious and legal affairs was Major Miljenko Jankovic. The assistant for logistics was Captain Predrag Slijepcevic. The chief of the office was a warrant office, Drago Mandic [as interpreted]. The commander of the Military Police Battalion was Zoran [Realtime transcript read in error "Smijlovic"] Malovic [as interpreted], major. The commander of the artillery rocket battalion was 2nd Lieutenant Nedeljko Jovicic, the commander of the tank company was Captain Rajko Knezevic. The commander of the Mixed Mortar Company and Battery was second Lieutenant Stevo Jevic. The commander of the Motorised Battalion was Captain First Class, I believe, Radivojevic, and I'm not sure if I mentioned any one of the commanders and commanding officers, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Just for the record, there is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Mr. Sarapa.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe in line 5, in fact, page 5, line 19, I believe the witness said "Malinic" and what we have on the record is "Mandic."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's all right, but I believe that it says here "Zoran Smijlovic." It should be "Zoran Malinic," battalion of the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Line 20.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Are you familiar with someone by the name of Aleksandar Lucic?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At that time, he was lieutenant or captain, I can't remember exactly, and his duty was deputy commander of the Military Police Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: With respect to the Military Police Battalion, where was that headquartered, where was it stationed?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The command of the battalion and the battalion itself, beginning with the second half of 1993, was stationed in Nova Kasaba on the Milici-Konjevic Polje-Zvornik road.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And approximately how many men did that comprise?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in the command of the battalion, together with the office administration, couriers, around ten persons, not more, including the soldiers who served there.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And how was the military -- I'm sorry. How was the Military Police Battalion organised?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Military Police Battalion had a command led by the commander, deputy commander, clerk for general duties, and some auxiliary personnel. That was the command. In addition to that, the battalion had four military police companies. The 1st Military Police Company was equipped and trained for anti-terrorist action. The 2nd Military Police Company was the company of armoured personnel carriers, and its primary purpose, in peace time, of course, was to keep law and order, to escort military leaders, control crowds, et cetera: The 3rd and 4th Companies of the Military Police were primarily to secure the command post, that is, a classical guard duty, patrol duty, use of specially-trained dogs, in military police patrols, et cetera. In addition to that, the battalion had a specialised unit that led the work of the duty service of the military police, and that's a service that I forgot to mention when I enumerated all the other units. That was the structure.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: With respect to each of these companies, can you tell us, in July of 1995 or thereabout, where they were located?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In July 1995, the battalion of military police was engaged as follows: The 1st Company and part of the 2nd Company of the Military Police were part of the combat group of the Protection Regiment located in Ocadjava area as part of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, that is, in the focus of the defence held by the SRK, and that's halfway between Sarajevo and Trnovo and in the area of Mount Treskavic. So I said that was the 1st Company and part of the 2nd Company, and part of the 4th Company also went into that combat group. The 3rd Company was doing regular guard duty of the command post, including the dogs, and part of the -- part of the armoured personnel carriers was at the Staff and some were on leave, on home leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: The APCs, the armoured personnel carriers, when you say they were at the Staff, do you mean they were at the command post of the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. They were at that time in the area of Nova Kasaba, at the base of the battalion. Let me just explain what I mean by military police APCs. They are lightly-armoured combat vehicles, armed only with one light machine-gun, 7.62 millimetres, used for military police personnel transport, to protect personnel from rifle and light machine-gun fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Thank you for that. Now, in the beginning of July, were the APCs located in Nova Kasaba or were they located at the Main Staff command post?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Early in July, or more precisely from the 26th of June onwards, that part of the unit, that is, part of the company of the APC, was at the HQ of the Main Staff, because on the 26th of June there was an attack by the 28th Division against the base of the Main Staff, the HQ of the Main Staff. Since I had not enough forces to defend the Main Staff, I ordered the commander of the Military Police Company, Major Malinic, to go to the area of the command post to defend the command post first and then take other necessary actions. So from the 26th of June onwards, they were on the command post of the Main Staff or, rather, the Protection Regiment, because that's the same location.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Now, you'd earlier mentioned that you didn't have an assistant commander for security. Could you explain for us the relationship of the Military Police Battalion and your regiment with the security organ of the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can explain. The battalion of the military police was part of the regiment. It was not an independent unit. And the battalion was commanded by the commander of the regiment, through the commander of the MP Battalion. I already said I didn't have an assistant for intelligence and security. What was envisaged for such cases by the rules, it was envisaged that the so-called security support, that is, counter-intelligence service, be performed by the relevant unit. Since the Protection Regiment belonged to the Staff, it was the most logical thing for the relevant organ of the Main Staff to perform that duty. The head of Administration would appoint one operations officer to take care of the counter-intelligence support for the Military Police Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And as it existed in July 1995, was there any specific relationship between the head of the Military Police Battalion of your regiment and officers in the security organ of the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly -- I didn't really understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Well, from whom did Major Malinic take his orders with respect to the administration of the Military Police Battalion within your regiment?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He got orders from me, as regiment commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And with respect to the disposition of the military police units, from whom did you receive your orders?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the commander of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And were the orders that you received from the commander of the Main Staff -- are they processed through a type of proposal that is made by officers of the security organ to the commander of the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that is precisely the role of security organs, that regardless of the level of command, they propose to the commander in which way to use military police units according to the situation. If you allow me maybe now or maybe later, I should say a few words about the tasks of the Administration for Security and security organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now would be a good time.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me put it this way: The security organ, and in this case I am talking about the security organs of the Main Staff, i.e., the Security Administration of the Main Staff, was a professional body of the Command of the Main Staff. Its duties were as follows: The first task that the Security Administration and its members had was to document, monitor and prevent any intelligence work by foreign intelligence services or any other bodies involved in intelligence against the Republika Srpska Army as a whole and its institutions, against its documents, plans, armies and equipment. That's the first task, to discover document and prevent the work of foreign intelligence bodies, and this is what only a professional body could do because they were the only ones that were trained to do that. The second task of the security organ was to discover, prevent, document any enemy activities against the Republika Srpska Army. The third task was to draft plans of counter-intelligence protection of the units, organs and institutions of the Army of Republika Srpska. Who was involved in all that? It was the counter-intelligence department with the Security Administration. That was involved in that. In addition to that, the administration for intelligence also had department of military police. What was its role? Its role was to professionally lead the units of military police. In that department of military police which was part of the -- of the Intelligence Administration, there were usually former officers of military police units who occupied all the relevant positions; in other words, there were experienced military policemen who were aware of the issues involved with the work of the military police, and their task was to be engaged in professional work, which ranged from drafting plans and programmes, combat training, equipping the military police units with special equipment that was necessary to carry out military police tasks, and so on and so forth. In other words, a direct link from the regiment command and the Intelligence Administration went through the department of the military police, when military policing was involved. Sometimes on a daily basis a lot of things happened. For example, the chief of the department would call the Command of the regiment and say that they needed escort for officers from the Main Staff; for example, that they needed two, three, to five patrols of members of the military police who would stay on duty for a few days. Food had to be provided for them. These were the tasks that were not imaginary. They were very concrete and very much happening every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you for that. If I could, I'd like to just direct your attention to late June, early July of 1995, with respect to the disposition of your units. Can you tell us what your assignment was with respect to your unit at the end of June of 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to go back to the overall assignments of the units of the Protection Regiment. I told you where parts of the Military Police Battalion were, they were assigned to the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps on the Sarajevo front line. In addition to them, there were also parts of the Motorised Battalion, Mixed Mortar Company, and one part of the Traffic Company. They were all there on that front line. The other units were deployed as follows: The artillery/rocket Division of the antiaircraft defence was in the sector of the command post of the Main Staff, providing combat duty office in case there was activity from the air. The tank company was in the barracks in Han Pijesak. Parts of the Motorised Battalion were deployed on positions facing the Zepa Brigade, i.e., facing the Zepa sector. The sabotage unit as well, which was a very small unit numbering some 20 men at the time, they were also part of the combat group. The logistic company was in Han Pijesak, performing tasks of logistical support for the combat group at the Sarajevo front line as well as for the other units which were deployed elsewhere. The regiment command was always at its command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Did you receive any orders at the end of June with respect to conducting any reconnaissance missions in that area, that is, in the area of the Main Staff Command.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honours, I have to say something before I answer. I said that from 12 October 1994 to 23rd June, I was hospitalised. On the 23rd of June, 1995, I returned to the command post of the regiment. I was briefed about the situation not only in the regiment but also in the entire territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And sometime in the afternoon, the commander of the Main Staff, General Mladic, and assistant for intelligence, General Tolimir, came to my command post. Having greeted each other and having exchanged some words about health and family, General Mladic told me that on the following day, on the 24th of June, I have to familiarise myself with the physical protection of the command post, because while I was absent from the unit some things were changed in the security system, so he ordered me to look at the situation to see whether the things that had been changed in the time were okay, and if my assessment was that they were not, that I should take measures in order to put things right and in order to improve the situation. I did that as ordered on the following day, and I concluded that some alterations had to be done to some technical positions, that some things had to be improved. On the 25th of June, I carried out preparations for those changes, and then on the 26th of June I ordered that the changes should be started. At the moment when this was being done, an attack on the command post of the Main Staff happened. As a result of that attack, I had seven dead soldiers and a large number of wounded soldiers and officers. One soldier was taken prisoner. And after that attack and after dealing with the sequela of the attack, I brought in part of the armoured company and the tank company. After that, I was ordered by the commander of the Main Staff to undertake intense reconnoitering activities in the direction of Zepa so as to prevent any other such unpleasant surprises as we had on the 26th of June. I said to the Commander that I don't have anybody free and that I would have to pull out at least one military police company from Ocadjava sector, that they would have to be very well trained, officers and soldiers with a lot of combat experience, in order to be -- to perform that task. This was approved, and when they arrived at the command post I undertook the activities that you asked me about.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Now, with respect to your assignment, did you carry that out, and on what axis did you carry that out, if so?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That assignment was being carried out. You cannot do it in a limited space of time. It's a continuous activity which is undertaken in order to establish the deployment of the enemy, the situation and the intention. I started performing that task after I had consolidated the situation at the command post, and I went on carrying it out until mid-July, when I was given another assignment, and I embarked on that assignment. In other words, I was performing that assignment towards the front line of the Zepa Brigade, starting from the Karavac village sector to the Drina River and the right neighbour, the neighbour on the right flank, which is the 1st Rogatica Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. I'm just going to ask you to slow down a little bit, because you do have a lot to say, but it's kind of hard to keep up with what you're saying. Now, with respect to discharging this assignment, can you tell us specifically what you did in relation to this reconnaissance that you were carrying out? Did you set up -- well, just tell us what you did, specifically.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This military police platoon was used to form three reconnoitering groups. I gave them their tasks, I sent them to their concrete axes, and their task was to establish whether the enemy was present on those axes. If they were, then they were given the task to establish what was their strength, what their intentions were, and so on and so forth. In other words, every day I would assign a new axis of movement. The tasks remained the same within the overall task of reconnoitering. Throughout all that time, there was no combat engagement with the enemy. We were able to establish that after the aforementioned attack, they returned to their sectors in which they were normally deployed before that attack. However, we had to keep the situation under control, because when you do things on time, in a planned manner and in an organised manner, it's easier to keep the situation under control than when you have to do it under attack. In other words, I had normal reconnoitering activities that followed the textbook tactic of reconnoitering activities, and I -- it would take me a long time to go into the details of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Your answer is just fine as it is. Now, from where were these activities carried out?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The basis for those scouting activities was the Crna Rijeka sector where the regiment was deployed, as well as the sector of the Rogatica Brigade, i.e., the area of responsibility of the Rogatica Brigade, Rogatica village, where we had the abilities to billet men after their tasks. So there were two bases. There were the Borike and Rogatica sectors where these tasks were performed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, you said that your assignment had changed at some point. Tell us when that occurred.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The second assignment, I was given automatic -- I discontinued my previous assignment, and I was given that assignment on the 4th of July, 1995. On that day, I was in the sector of the Sjeversko village towards Boksanica, this is where I was at the forward command post of the brigade, and I was given the task to report to the sector of Laze village. That's from Borike, in the direction of the sector of the command post of the Main Staff. And I was told to report to the Barrier 01, which was the code name for the commander of the Main Staff. On my way to that sector, I came across units of the Drina Corps. I saw the chief of Staff of the Drina Corps, Colonel Svetozar Andric there. We greeted each other briefly, and I received my orders from the commander of the Main Staff. The orders were to take the unit that was with me, which was a military police platoon, to carry out an attack on the Laze-Gusinac-Brezova Ravan axis, to break up the combat security of the Zepa Brigade in the Gusinac sector, and later on to take the sector of Brezova Ravan.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, were you situated in Borike at some point during July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And from when to when was that?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All this time, throughout all these scouting activities, I was using those two bases, one on the right border and the other on the left border. I used Crna Rijeka because I had conditions there to billet the troops, and if I was closer to Borike, I would sleep at Borike. For example, I would be in the Borike sector on the 5th and the 6th, and then on the 7th and the 8th I would be in Crna Rijeka. I would shift between these two positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: During the time you were in Borike, did you -- were there other members of the Main Staff that were also staying there?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the beginning of my stay there, there was nobody, and later on, I can't be sure of the date, the assistant commander of the Main Staff for intelligence and security, General Drago Tolimir, arrived at the Borike sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: How long did General Tolimir stay there?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 14th, I was given the second assignment. He remained at the Borike sector, and from then on I really didn't have a possibility to know where he was, whether he remained in Borike, whether he was in Rogatica or in Crna Rijeka. I really don't know. The next time I saw him was after the end of combat activities around Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did anybody else from the Main Staff stay in Borike during the time that you were there?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, the facilities at Borike, in terms of communication with your units, were you able to communicate with your units while you were there?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With some of the units, I had a direct telephone line. As for the Command in the Crna Rijeka sector and the battalion of the military police, as well. With the others, I did not have direct contact. I'm talking about those units that were on the Sarajevo and Romanija front line. That communication went through the Command and the Corps Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: For Borike itself, did you have the facility -- the ability, I should say, to communicate by radio, for example, with your units?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I only had a telephone connection through a radio equipment, RIU1. I had communication with the Command in the Crna Rijeka sector and the battalion of the military police. That's who I had communication with.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, in order to make contact with your troops while you were in Borike, did you have to go someplace else in order to, for example, communicate by teletype?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember having had the need to send any documents in such a way. The unit that was assigned to the Sarajevo Romanija Corps had been resubordinated to the Corps Command and was being given its tasks from them, so there was no need for me to send any orders in that direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Well, I'm not talking about orders, particularly. I'm just talking about communication, in general.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I had had to do that, I had at my disposal the communications equipment of the Rogatica Brigade, so I'm sure that I would have been able to use those.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, I just want to draw your attention, if I could, specifically to July 13th. Were you in contact with Zoran Malinic on that day?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was in contact, in telephone contact with him, to be precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And where were you at the time that you were in telephone contact with him, and where was he, as best as you recall?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was in Nova Kasaba, and I was in the sector of Sjeversko village. Borike is a more general and better-known term that we normally use, but to be more precise, I was in the vicinity of the village of Borike.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And in relation to -- did you have a conversation with Mr. Malinic?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Major Malinic called me in the morning on that day. It was in the early morning hours. I can't remember when. He told me that in the Nova Kasaba sector, there were two or three prisoners of war already by then. That's what he told me. And he also told me that he had some members of the Dutch Battalion of UNPROFOR who turned to Major Malinic for help because of the combat activities that had taken place in the Srebrenica sector. They did not feel safe to return to their base in Potocari. They came to the barracks and stayed there for the next two or three days. I said, "Okay, make sure that those people were safe." And as for the prisoners of war, treated them as is prescribed by the rules of the military police; put them in adequate facilities and put them under your protection. I have to say that at that moment, Major Malinic had at his disposal no more than 15 men in the Nova Kasaba sector. There was him, a few couriers, the duty service of the military police with a couple of military policemen, and some of the logistics platoon. In other words, there was some 50 [as interpreted] or so men there, and it should not have been a problem to control two or three men who had surrendered. In other words, they were not captured, because until that moment we never left the barracks. These men came on their own to surrender and to seek protection from our unit. Shall I continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'll just ask you another question, if I could. First, is what you've related to us what he specifically told you when you had this conversation with him?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Petrusic, you know I could see you because of the column. The next time you stand up, someone please draw our attention. Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, there is an error in the transcript at page 20, line 11. It should read "15" rather than "50." The witness said that there were some 15 men there, and it has been recorded as "50." May this be corrected, please. Line 9, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I remember the witness specifically saying "15," not "50," so that will be corrected. Thank you, Mr. Petrusic. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: My question was whether or not what you've related to us is specifically what was related to you in this conversation, or is this information that you learned subsequently?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The information that I shared with you, i.e., when he told me that he had one or two prisoners, or three prisoners of war, i.e., people who had surrendered, and a couple of members of the Dutch Battalion of UNPROFOR, he shared this with me in that telephone conversation, which means I did not learn that subsequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, the telephone conversation that you had, was that over a PTT line or was that done over a radio relay line or radio line?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that the only possibility I had to communicate was a radio relay line, using the telephone RRU1 line. I did not have a PTT connection. There was a problem with telephone lines over there, anyway. I really don't know what it was about, but I did not have a regular PTT line.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did you have any further conversations with Major Malinic during the course of that day, that is, the 13th of July?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And when was the next conversation -- well, first let me ask you, this conversation you had in the morning, about what time was that, if you can recall?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've just told you, it was in the morning, but I really can't tell you whether it was at 8.00 or 9.00 or when. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: When was the next conversation that you had with Major Malinic?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure about the time, again, but again Major Malinic called me. And then he relayed to me the following information: The situation was getting more complex over there; there was a continuous stream of larger groups of people, mostly members of the 28th Division from Srebrenica who were surrendering, and he was facing a problem. He could not protect those people. He could not protect his men, let alone the prisoners. I told him to call the regiment command and that the company of armoured PCs that was at the command post as of the 26th of June should be sent to the Nova Kasaba sector. I'm talking about some 30 men or so, and their task should have been to reinforce his forces and provide protection for the deployment area, to provide protection for his own men, equipment and the rest. And again I drew his attention to the fact that the prisoners of war should be treated according to the rules of service, that he should take care of his own safety and security, and then that he should also make sure that security and safety should be provided for those people who had surrendered. Your Honours, I have to say something here that you may not be aware of. After that conversation we had, Major Malinic took the following measures: Since among the people who had surrendered, there were some who were wounded and injured, he called up the war hospital in Milici and asked for a medical team to come urgently to extend first aid. Second, he asked from the command of the Milici Brigade that if they had any reserves of bread and other food, that they should send it to the area of Nova Kasaba so that it can be given to the people who, as he saw it, had not eaten for a while and had not even had water for a long time. Despite his efforts, he said that he had been informed that there would also be television teams coming from Republika Srpska, so Major Malinic took that series of measures. He also started registering, listing the prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Was all of this that you've just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Mr. Vanderpuye, that despite his efforts -- [Previous translation continues...] I love it, so I won't stop her. There, despite his efforts, in line 9 on page 23, it doesn't sound right to me there.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note: The witness started saying one thing, and then he moved to another thing, so it turned into a very clumsy sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I understand that, and I thank you for it. But did you ultimately get the medical -- did Malinic get the medical team that he requested and the food, the bread? Did that arrive or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That did arrive. The medical team performed its job, did the triage, and extended medical assistance, some food and water arrived, so the request the major asked for was not just formal, it was something that was done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Yes, Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, one correction to the transcript, page 23, lines 9 to 11. The witness said, and it's missing, the television teams not from Republika Srpska showed up in the field. They were foreign television crews. We see the contrary in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Was Malinic informed that there would also be television teams coming from Republika Srpska or coming from elsewhere, but not Republika Srpska? What was the information he received?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The information I received was that television crews were coming from several major television companies from the world. They were major television companies, and unfortunately we, locally, do not have one that would count as a major one on the world scene.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. Savcic, you -- was all this information that you've related to us just now, is that information you actually received from Mr. Malinic when you had the conversation with him or is this information that you subsequently learned?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That information on the measures taken I learned later, but I've already said that in that second telephone conversation, he told me the situation was getting more and more complex. More and more people were surrendering, and that's an important distinction. He did not have enough forces to take prisoners, because that would require performing searches, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I just want the record to be clear as to what it is he told you versus what it is you know, so that's the reason I'm asking you these questions. Did you learn about this list of registered prisoners that he made during the course of that conversation or did you learn about that at some other point?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Later, subsequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: With respect to this list, do you know where or what he did with it, or where it could have been found or has been found?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I met with Malinic on the 27th of July, 1995. On the 27th of July, I was asked to come to the command post of the Main Staff, and General Miletic passed on to me the orders of the commander of the Main Staff, that I should go immediately to the area of Drvar, which is 500 kilometres away from Crna Rijeka, because there had been a serious aggravation in that part of the theatre of war. And as I was passing through Nova Kasaba, I had my first opportunity ever to stop by the command of the battalion to see Malinic, and on that occasion we spent about half an hour discussing the recent events in Kasaba.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Is that when he told you about the request for triage and food and water?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. So he took that order I had issued. He acted according to the rules of the service. And in that situation, it was his assessment that those measures were called for and that they were in keeping both with my order and the rules and provisions governing treatment of POWs.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And is that when he told you about the foreign television crews or the major television crews that were to be at that location?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And during your conversation with Mr. Malinic on the 13th, while you were in Borike, do you know where General Tolimir was?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think -- in fact, I know he was somewhere there. He might even have been standing next to me. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And do you know whether or not he was aware of the situation that Major Malinic was relating to you on the telephone at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He knew. He was aware of that if only from the conversation I had with Malinic. But whether he also had communications with other people in that broader area, I couldn't tell you. As for the events in Nova Kasaba, he knew about that. He was around, standing next to me. But I don't know about any other communications he might have had.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned that Major Malinic had made a request for additional units, and I believe you've indicated that they arrived. Did he make that request of you or did he make the request of somebody else?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So when we were talking on the phone, I told him to call up the command of the regiment in Crna Rijeka, that is, Lieutenant-Colonel Jazic, and to make the request. It's not actually units, it's part of the APC Unit that had 30 men who were in Crna Rijeka, reinforcing security, and they were now returning to their initial location because the situation had, in the meantime, changed for the worse in Kasaba and it had improved in the command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Is there any reason, in particular, why you didn't order it yourself, given the fact that he had made the request or communicated his -- communicated the request to you directly?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, just the technical reason, and the technical reason was that this radio relay is more difficult to establish, it's not so good as stationary telephone, as the land line, and I told him to do that part of the job because he had better communications equipment at that moment than I.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And in order for these -- in order for these APCs to be moved from Crna Rijeka to Nova Kasaba, that would have to be approved, I take it, by you or somebody else. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I gave my approval for that move, and they were performing, in doing so, their primary task. They were providing security for elements of the combat disposition of the Main Staff, and they were moving to Kasaba, where they were needed at that time. And they were the quickest to arrive with their own vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, did that require the approval of the higher command, that is, the command -- the commander, I should say, General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it did not. It did not, because I was not issuing a new task to the battalion or, rather, part of the battalion. It was just moving to a different location while continuing to perform its primary task, that is, security service, security provided to an installation and an area. If I had wanted to issue them a completely new task that is not envisaged in the basic plan of use, then I would have required approval from the superior command.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: With respect to the first conversation that you had with Mr. Malinic, Major Malinic, he indicated to you there was two or three prisoners. Now, with respect to the second conversation, did he tell you approximately how many, even though you've described that the situation was worsening, did he tell you approximately how many prisoners he had on his hands?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember him mentioning a specific number, a figure. He said there were many, there were many, and with the forces he had in the area of Kasaba, he was completely helpless.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Is it time for the break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And in actual fact, once you've raised the issue, we will be proceeding beyond quarter to 4.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: No problem. JUDGE AGIUS. Till five to 4.00, and then we will have a 30-minute break at five to 4.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, in his request for reinforcements, is it your testimony that he made no mention as to how many prisoners he was dealing with?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, but I think that misstates the evidence. I don't think that there was a request. I believe this witness has testified that when he talked to Malinic, that he told Malinic what to do, to call the command post. So I think that misstates the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I don't think it misstates the evidence at all, but I'll be happy to rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then rephrase it, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: When you spoke to Major Malinic, did he make a request for reinforcements or help in controlling the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course he did, because he said there were many of them. I don't remember him giving me a figure. It's difficult to make an assessment. It later turned out, and we reached a figure of 1.200 people, but then all he was saying was, "I have many of them, and with the men I have, I can't do anything, I can't provide security for our personnel, let alone the prisoners of war." So these people who had surrendered were in the open air, next to the thoroughfare that had not been closed down yet. There was traffic continuing on it. And if I understood you correctly in your question, he was asking for help. I knew at that moment that I had no more backup to send him than that APC Company. The tank company was difficult to send. They would take a long time, and it was not their job because this was not a combat activity. So I had nothing to send him.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Well, how many APCs did you send or were sent, I should say?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, how many did we have, six?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And how many men would that be?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you, 30.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Now, you know some of the accused in this case; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know all of them. I know all the accused in this case. The least well I know, Mr. Dragan Nikolic. In fact, I know him very little.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And could you -- could you tell us what your relationship is with General Pandurevic?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Pandurevic and I belong to the same generation. We were born in 1957. We were born in Sokolac. He's just a few months older. We graduated together from the military academy. We met in 1978, in the first year of our studies, and practically from that day we have been very good friends. That friendship was based first on the fact that we came from the same part of the country. Later, it became a closer friendship. I baptized his children. I was his best man, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. You know Colonel Beara?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly. I first met Colonel Beara in the second half of 1992, I think around this time of year, September/October. He was chief of the Security Administration at the Main Staff. We know each other well. I don't know what other details you would like about this relation.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. As the chief of security, he reported to General Tolimir; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was his immediate superior, so logically he was the one to inform about the duties he had carried out and to receive new tasks, although in principle it's the commander of the unit to which the security organs belonged that handles security activities. So security organs at a higher level lead and govern the work of lower-standing security organs. That is the chain.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. You know General Miletic?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know him. I also know him from mid-1992, when, as I seem to recall, he was a lieutenant-colonel when he arrived at the Main Staff, to become chief of artillery rocket units. And in that first contact -- and I remember clearly the day when he arrived. I remember he helped me a lot in establishing this artillery rocket battalion, because I did not have experience with that. I got the necessary resources and equipment. We later effected reinforcement, filled it with men, and General Miletic was an exemplary worker who was rewarded for his work by appointment to become chief of operations and training at the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And you respect General Miletic; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. I respect all of them. They are my comrades in arms, and I have great respect for all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, you and I have spoken about your testimony prior to today, but have you spoken to anybody else regarding your testimony since you've arrived here in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Apart from talking to you, I spoke to the Defence teams of General Miletic, General Pandurevic and General Gvero. I think that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Could I have 65 ter 192, please, in e-court?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Do you see this document up on the screen, Mr. Savcic?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Have you seen that document before?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have. The first time I saw it was when I spoke to Mr. McCloskey in Banja Luka less than two years ago, and on that occasion I said what I thought of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. This is a document -- if we could just page down -- that bears your name; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And if we could just go to the top, it indicates forward command post of the 65th Protection Regiment at the top and a location of Borike, and a time of 1400 hours. Do you have any specific recollection of having prepared this document yourself?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We have discussed it even here, after I got here to the Tribunal. You showed the bottom of the page a moment ago. It's true, my name is there, but there is no signature. So I've already told you that I don't recall drafting this document myself, and here are a few reasons why I still can't believe I did: First of all, in the heading it says "IKM Forward Command Post of the 65th Protection Regiment," et cetera, "Borike, 1400 hours." I did not set up that forward command post. I just led part of that unit that was there. There is no date indicated. This document does not have the format of a telegram, whereas it was supposed to be sent by telegram to the addresses indicated. Next, I cannot suggest something to the commander of the Main Staff or his deputy, because I'm not an assistant commander to suggest and propose. I'm just a subordinate who executes the missions given him. Furthermore, you see, after the first sentence, it says: "Assistant commander of the Main Staff of the VRS for intelligence and security proposes the following measures." So the assistant commander proposes, and I'm the one writing. If he is the one proposing, then why he isn't -- why isn't he the one who's writing? Then I've just noticed that names of units start in small letters, not capitals. That's something that I know. So I cannot say with any certainty that I drafted this, as dictated by Tolimir, but I cannot refute the possibility with 100 per cent certainty, either. I can just say that this document was never received by the commander of the military police, and the commander of the military police never acted upon it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Well, how can you say that it was never received by the commander of the military police? On what information can you make that statement?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I base that on the statement by Major Malinic. He was 100 per cent convinced that he had never received this and that he had never acted upon this order, because he was never aware of this order.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: When did you speak to Major Malinic about this specific order? Was it after you spoke to Mr. McCloskey in 2005?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And on how many occasions did you discuss this particular order with Mr. Malinic or anybody else, for that matter?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. I didn't quite understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Maybe --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It's a difficult question. It should be broken down into, one Malinic, and, two, anyone else, I would suggest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for that suggestion.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: It's well taken. I will do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: On how many occasions did you speak to Major Malinic about this order?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once. I was interested whether he remembered this order. He said that he didn't have a clue, that he didn't remember. Not only did he not remember, but he was convinced and he claimed that no telegram bearing my signature arrived at his position on that day or ever, for that matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Did you speak to anybody else regarding this order between the time that you spoke to Mr. McCloskey in 2005 and the time that you first came here a few days ago?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, nobody. Why would I speak to anybody else if those people didn't have anything to do with these things? Here you can see the list of addressees, whom I could not contact, and it would have been totally pointless of me to talk to people who had nothing whatsoever to do with the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. And when you spoke to Mr. -- to Major Malinic about this particular order, did you discuss with him the specifics of its contents; that is, the text, what it talks about?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. To be honest, I didn't. The document was not available to me. I didn't have it on me. Mr. McCloskey had shown it to me in Banja Luka, and we had discussed this document. So I did not go into the contents of the document. I just inquired about the existence of the document. I asked him whether he remembered that he received a telegram from me on the 13th of July. Since he said that he didn't, I really didn't go into the details or the contents of the document. I just told him that it referred to the treatment of prisoners of war. I really did not try to retain the contents, bullet point by bullet point, so I could not discuss the details with anybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Were you able to determine who the signalsman was with respect to the transmission of this particular document?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I'm afraid I didn't understand your question. Could you repeat it, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Would a document normally -- like this normally be sent via teletype or through a signalsman?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As we look at the heading and the addressees, we see that it had to be sent through the Main Staff, which means that it had to be encrypted on the teleprinting machine of the closest unit that was able to establish a teleprinter communication with the next closest unit. What I'm saying is that things should have been done in that way, with a caveat that I really don't remember ever having sent this document or given it to somebody for transmission.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Can we just page down on the document in e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Do you see an indication, on the left-hand bottom of that document of a time and date?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And what does that refer to?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Handed over -- signals and communications are not my specialty. I don't know what this refers to, whether this refers to whether this -- to the moment when this document was received or transmitted. I really can't be sure. I don't know whether this means that this document was received at that time or whether it was given for encrypted or -- whether it was encrypted at that moment or transmitted to a different point for encrypting. I really don't know. Again, I don't see a stamp here. This is handwriting. There is a signature here, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. You can't determine from the signature who it is; is that fair to say?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't determine, from the signature, who that is, because I did not have my own signalsman, so I really wouldn't know. The logic makes me believe that if this had been transmitted, it should have been done by somebody from the Rogatica Brigade. There were no other units here. It could not have been, let's say, the 16 Krajina whatever from somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, with respect to the content of the document itself, if I could just refer you to paragraph number 3. Paragraph number 3 reads: "Commander of the Military Police Battalion shall take measures to remove war prisoners from the main Ilicici-Zvornik road, place them somewhere indoors or in an area protected from observation from the ground or the air." Now, you recall having been put questions concerning that paragraph back in 2005 when you spoke to the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And, in particular, do you recall having been asked what military reason you could think of that all of these prisoners, a thousand prisoners, would have to be protected from observation from the air?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that question as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Do you remember what your answer was?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember my answer was that when it came to the protection from observation from the air, that there was a constant threat coming from the NATO Air Force and that there could have been collateral damage in any of those campaigns. That's what I was talking about, and I was talking about a possible mistake as a result of fire from the air.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And do you stand by that answer, the answer that you gave back in 2005?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was never excluded as a possibility. Things happen, mistakes happen. I'm not talking about anybody's intentional shelling of human targets. The way I'm thinking is a pilot of an M-16 MiG, can he see whether the people down there are armed or not armed, whether they represent a tactical group or something? In other words, saying that this did not have to be somebody's planned activity, that a mistake could have happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you. This would be a good time to break now, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How much more time do you need to conclude your direct?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I think a good half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. We'll have a 30-minute break starting from now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. Savcic, I just want to bring something to your attention, and maybe you can help clarify this. Earlier on in your testimony, when you were talking about the relationship between the security organ and the military police, it appears in the transcript, and maybe it's a translation issue, but it appears in the transcript that you said that there was a direct link from the regiment command and the Intelligence Administration that went through the department of the military police when military policing was involved. And that's on page 11 for my friends --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please, could counsel speak into the microphone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Sorry. That's on page 11, lines 20 through 23, 23. The entire paragraph actually runs much longer than that, but that's the part that I would ask the witness to explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Do you subscribe to that? Is that a correct interpretation of what you said?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see that on the screen. I can't see what it says there. I really can't. Can you help me with that respect? Can you be more specific? Can you be clear and say what exactly it is that is stated in the transcript?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The witness doesn't need to bother with the transcript page, et cetera. You go there, please. Read it out slowly, and it will be translated word for word to him in his language.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In the meantime, the other teams have the reference, and they can read it accordingly.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes. Just to give it a bit of content, I will read from line 10 down. Maybe that would be better. It says: "In addition to that," talking about the relationship of the security organ or the function of the security organ: "In addition to that, the --" it says "also had a military police. What was its role? Its role was to professionally lead the units of military police, and that department of military police which was part of the Intelligence Administration, there were usually former officers of the Intelligence Administration --" I'm sorry -- "former officers of the military police units who occupied all the relevant positions. In other words, there were experienced military policemen who were aware of the issues involved with the work of the military police, and their task was to be engaged in professional work, which ranged from drafting plans and programmes, combat training, equipping the military police units with special equipment that was necessary to carry out military police tasks, and so on and so forth. In other words, a direct link from the regiment command and the Intelligence Administration went through the department of the military police when military policing was involved." Now, I know that was a pretty long passage, but what seems to be coming out of that is essentially that the relationship between the military police and the security organ --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Finish the question. Witness, don't start answering the question, because we need to hear what Mr. Meek has to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: -- was limited to the intelligence aspect of that order, and I wondered if that's what you meant or whether you could clarify that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, but now it's too late for me to object. So ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, it's -- why is it too late for you to object?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Well, because, first off, it's an improper question. He's trying to ask a question in a leading and suggestive manner insofar as what he says is, "It seems to be coming out of this," well, it seemed to him to be that way, it can seem to me to be a different way, it can seem to the Judges to be even a third way, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's precisely why a clarification is needed. That's precisely why a clarification is needed. Yes, Mr. Savcic, have you understood Mr. Vanderpuye's question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Then please continue to give your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The only way I can understand this is a mistake in interpretation. Mr. Vanderpuye is repeating the word "Intelligence Administration," which is an entirely different segment of military activity. I have not mentioned the Intelligence Administration at all. I have mentioned the Security Administration, and I said that the main tasks of the Security Administration are threefold, saying that the bulk of the administration is involved in that, and the three tasks are discovering, documenting and preventing enemy intelligence activity. The second task is to discover, monitor and document any enemy activity. And the third part, pertaining to counter-intelligence, is providing counter-intelligence measures or protection for the entire army and its components based on the intelligence gathered. In practical terms, I'm talking about the structure of the Security Administration. In addition to the counter-intelligence tasks that are performed by specially-trained and educated security organs. The Administration also has on its strength a unit of military police or a department of military police which is engaged in professional matters of military policing at the level of the army, not only at the level of the regiment. And I said what their task is. The Administration for Security is -- carries the tactical development of the police, and hence its obligation towards the units of military police, starting with education, equipment, and so on and so forth. This is what I stated. In other words, and I repeat, although I have not emphasised that especially so far, there's no command line there. I -- if I needed to talk to the Security Administration, I had to send requests. For example, a request to equip the units of the military police, that would be my request in which I would list all the requirements. The Administration would then look at that and would provide the funds in a foreseeable period of time. In other words, there's no command function. Their role is professional, at the level of the battalion and no instructions or programmes can be drafted. I don't know whether I've made myself -- if that was possible, then the role of commander would be obsolete. This would mean duplicating facilities. One more sentence, please, if I may. I know that you have been involved in these issues for a long time, but let me tell you that the relationship between the security organ and the military police, i.e., the unit of military police, is absolutely the same as the relationship of any chief of any branch, for example, the chief of Engineers, the chief of Artillery, the chief of Communications, the chief of Chemical Protection. They are professionals who give suggestions to the commander on the use of respective units. And the same relationship is between the security organ and the military police. There is no other relationship. For that matter, there is a book of rules and regulations that we followed, and there was no room for improvisation there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are you happy with that answer, Mr. Vanderpuye?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, I am. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So let's move to the next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Before we left off, I had -- I had you look at this document, and that is the proposal with respect to -- made by the assistant commander for Security and Intelligence. Now, I had asked you about what you had previously said regarding paragraph 3, in terms of an explanation for why prisoners would be -- would need to be protected from the air, and you've given your answer. Is there anything you'd care to add to that explanation?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I would like to add that subsequently reflecting on that bullet point, with the caveat that this document is authentic and that it originated the way it is stated herein, as I was thinking about this document, I came to a conclusion why these measures should have been necessary, and let me give you my reasons. It arises from the bullet point 3, where the prisoners of war were. They were close to the main road, and there was traffic on that road. Those people were coming from the areas of Srebrenica, Milici, Bratunac, Zvornik. Those people had lived there. They knew each other. Unfortunately, from 1992 there were atrocious crimes happening on both sides, and it was possible that some people recognised each other, that there was some knee-jerk reactions on the part of individuals or groups. So that would be one of the reasons. The second reason would be that these people could not have remained in the open, in days 24 hours long, in July, half of that time is daylight, less than that is night. During the night, it is very difficult to provide security for so many people in such a large area in the conditions of low visibility, with only 15 or 30 men. The next thing that I would like to say is how this is regulated by the rules. I believe that if this came as a proposal from the assistant commander for Security, he must have had in mind certain provisions of the Geneva Conventions that provided for the protection of prisoners of war, also stipulates that they should not be exposed to the general public, and I believe that the assistant commander for Intelligence and Security, with a caveat that the document originated from him, had all that in mind, and this was my first reaction when I looked at the text. Now, the question before the break was why the prisoners should be protected from the air. That's why the first part of my answer went in that direction, and now I have added all the other reasons and all the other thoughts that I have about the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right, thank you. Thank you for that. If I could have 65 ter 236(2)(b). Are you able to read what's on the screen before you? If we could just page down a little bit. If you're not able to read it, I can -- we can provide a typewritten version of it. So just let me know and we'll proceed.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just tell me, there are two parts here. Do you mean the upper part or the lower part? There's "895" at the top and there is "854300."

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: The lower of the two, "854300," if you could just page down so it's at the top of the page. You know what, I think it would be better if we used the typed version. If we could, Mr. President, could we go into private session for a moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's do that. Let's go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And as Judge Kwon is pointing out, we could also remain in public session and not broadcast the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That's fine. What I prefer to do is use the typed version of it, and I understand that it's under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. But before proceeding this way, I want to make sure there is no opposition from anyone. We hear none, so let's go back to open session with the understanding that this document will be not transmitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session, Witness, and Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Could I have instead 65 ter 2362C in e-court. Okay, we'll need to go to page 3 of that document and the bottom of the page as well. Okay, I think that's much better.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I just want to direct your attention to the section below where it says "14.05."

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, this is an intercept that refers to, among other things, a soccer field. It refers to a telegram and is dated the 13th of July with a time indicated of 14.05. Given the context and the information that's contained in this document, does it appear to you that the reference to the telegram is a telegram that you've just looked at in e-court?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second, Mr. Vanderpuye. Do we have an English translation?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: We do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The number seems to be wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. I'll track it down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Whilst there's a hiatus, we would suggest that the question just asked is a leading one, and when it's re-asked, could it be rephrased, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Josse. What do you have to say to that, Mr. Vanderpuye?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'm a bit preoccupied, I'm sorry, and I can't recall the precise wording of the question. All right, I now see it on the screen and I can rephrase it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, all right. It's line 7 to 12, anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You can read it for yourself. Is there a problem, Mr. Vanderpuye?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
