utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm sorry, I was just trying to locate the English translation of the intercept in e-court. I have a hard copy of it, and perhaps I can put that on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Rephrasing the question, in which case Mr. Josse has rephrased it for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. I think everyone can see the English translation now.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. Savcic, looking at that intercept, do you see any relationship between the subject matter and the telegram that you've just looked at?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, it's a very short conversation. The only argument that would support the connection between this intercept and the telegram is the football pitch, but there's a problem there. The problem in the time when this originated. It looks like the telegram was first written at 1400 hours, and then the conversation took place at 14.05, when the information was passed on the basis of which the telegram was written. It's not particularly logical, that last expression used there, meaning, "All right, let's do it," but that's not an expression I use, for instance. But there is a time discrepancy, 1400 hours for the telegram and 14.05 for the conversation. If the telegram took place or, rather, was written later, then it would have been more logical. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Let me show you 65 ter 2361. That would be C for the typed version, also under seal, and then there's A which should be the English translation. That's also on the third page of the document. At the top of the page. It actually precedes the one we looked at a minute ago. Could I just direct your attention to this intercept, and if you could, please read it to yourself.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean this conversation? I see "R-100."

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Do you see where it says "1400"?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Sorry, I'm just referring to you what's below that, if you could just read that conversation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Scroll it down, please.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, with respect to this intercept, do you see any relationship between this intercept and the telegram that you've just looked at in e-court?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, the only connection can be the reference to the football pitch and the number, "1.000."

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, there's a reference to somebody in this intercept by the name of Zoka. Do you know who that is?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who Zoka is.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Do you know if Zoran Malinic had a nickname that he used, whether it was -- did he have a nickname?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did, and his nickname was "Zoka," but that's a very common way to shorten the name of "Zoran," and all Zorans or almost all of them are referred to as "Zoka," but I don't know about the rest. This says Rade and Zoka and others had come. Bosko as well, somebody named Bosko, names that I'm not familiar with.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Thank you for that. Now, you indicated that on the 14th of July, you encountered or you met Svetozar Andric and you received further orders with respect to the disposition of your unit towards Zepa. Could you just describe for us briefly what you did, where you were, in relation to the operation towards Zepa?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could I have this left screen turned on so I can follow when the interpretation is finished? It's fine, it's fine now. So what I said is correct. I did meet with Mr. Svetozar Andric under the following circumstances: I was summoned by General Mladic and ordered to go to the area of Laze village, and on the way I ran into Mr. Andric. I stopped and greeted him, and he told me that the Drina Corps had received an assignment to make sure that the boundaries of Zepa are brought to the limits envisaged by the agreement. I have to say that on that part of the front line, there is a Motorised Battalion from the Protection Regiment. Its combat disposition is oriented towards the Zepa Brigade. When the Drina Corps units came by, Mr. Andric told the most senior officer in that Motorised Battalion, Gojko Petrusic, to show him the combat disposition of the forces in front of the battalion. When they tried to do that, the opposite side fired on them. Gojko Petrusic got killed, so those forces remained on the positions they had reached before that. I said before that I had received orders from General Mladic to use my combat disposition of my battalion to attack in Gusinac and Brezova Ravan direction and capture Brezova Ravan. I immediately proceeded to make preparations for that assignment on the 14th of July, and I did the following: Since we were facing strong, fortified positions, I couldn't capture them just by using infantry, so through the Command of the Drina Corps I requested that two combat -- two firing groups be formed for me, one group of mortars of 120 millimetres from the Bratunac Brigade and another firing group, two cannons, B1, from the Rogatic Brigade. In my request, I indicated where these two groups should be positioned, and that's what I did on the 14th of July. There were no other activities that I could manage, in view of the time of day when I received my assignment, because the terrain was very inhospitable, so that these two firing groups were set up, according to my request, at 1600 hours on the next day, the 15th.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And from the 15th through the 25th of July, what was your unit generally engaged in? And I'm only asking for a brief response, if you can.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 15th of July, with a fire of this firing group of cannons, B1, I neutralised the forces in Gusinac and captured that area. In the next period up to the 25th of July, fierce combat raged for the feature of Brezova Ravan.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And did you participate in those combat activities with respect to Brezova Ravan?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I'm talking about. From the 15th to the 25th of July, there was fierce fighting for the capture of that feature, and I was directly involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Was the feature captured? Was it captured on that day?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember the date exactly, but it must have been the 24th or the 25th of July. I can't be sure which of the two.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And following its capture, did you enter Zepa, you or your units?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Neither my units or other units entered Zepa on that day because we had a decisive order from General Mladic that units must not go into Zepa. Practically from the moment when the enemy lost Brezova Ravan, organised resistance and organised defence of Zepa and the Zepa Brigade ceased. I entered Zepa myself on that day. I went to the check-point of the UNPROFOR in Zepa, stayed there a very short time, returned to the area of Brezova Ravan, where I received orders from General Mladic to move with my unit to the barracks in Han Pijesak and to be there in reserve, as backup, in order to intervene in case of emergency.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Just bear with me one moment. Thank you very much, Mr. Savcic. I have no further questions for you at this time. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vanderpuye. Let's go through the list of estimated cross-examinations. Madame Fauveau, you had requested an hour and a half.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, we will try to stay within that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Krgovic, you had requested an hour and a half.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I suspect we'll be less than that, Your Honour. It partly depends on questions that others ask. I'm optimistic we'll be less than an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Sarapa?

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Around five minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic? Sorry, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we were reckoning with 30 minutes, at most.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I will have no questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's wise. Thank you. Mr. Meek?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Your Honour, very few questions, maybe five minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, Mr. Meek. Mr. Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I need five minutes as well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So that gives us one hour and a half. Okay. Mr. Petrusic, would you like to go first?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't mind going first, but we don't have an agreement between Defence teams. If you request it, then of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, you start first.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Savcic. My name is Zoran Zivanovic, and in these proceedings I appear for Vujadin Popovic. I have just a few questions for you. They relate to the 25th and the 26th of June that you spoke about; namely, the dates when your units suffered losses, when seven of your soldiers were killed and a certain number was wounded. Could you just clarify for me, who inflicted those losses on your unit?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The losses were inflicted by the forces of the 28th Division of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina from Srebrenica, from Srebrenica and Zepa, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Were your troops outside the enclaves, practically in the territory held by the Army of Republika Srpska at the time when they were attacked and when the unit suffered these losses?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were physically securing the command post of the Main Staff. That is way outside the territory controlled by the Muslim forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you give us an estimate of the distance from the enclave of Srebrenica or Zepa?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what could it be? I passed that way many times and never paid attention, but if we can translate it into different measures, how many hours on foot from the first line of Muslim defence to the place of attack, it takes at least two hours of fast walking.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell me, those units that attacked your troops, they came precisely from the enclaves?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zivanovic. Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. I'm Chris Meek, and I represent Ljubisa Beara. I just have a few questions. Sir, do you recall, when you spoke with Malinic that he never mentioned Ljubisa Beara being in Nova Kasaba?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he didn't mention Ljubisa Beara or anyone else. Later, I told you, when I stopped by on the 27th of July, he told me that the commander had been there, and I don't remember him mentioning anyone else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And when you say "the commander," isn't it a fact that Malinic told you that General Mladic had been there and spoken to the prisoners of war on the soccer pitch on the 13th?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He told me that General Mladic had arrived with his security men. He made a brief speech to the prisoners on the football pitch. He told them that they would all be exchanged. He said to Malinic that trucks and buses would be arriving shortly, that prisoners would be put on those vehicles and sent to Bratunac. As soon as that happened, any role of the units of the Protection Regiment ceased. And I have to emphasise that the Dutch Battalion of the UNPROFOR was there throughout.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now, you've just testified recently about the July 14th meeting where you ran into Colonel Andric. Do you recall that testimony, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Isn't it true, sir, that that was the first time that you learned that Drina Corps units were in the area?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And, further, you encountered General Krstic and General Blagojevic there; isn't that true, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that I met up with Colonel Blagojevic on the same day as Andric, but I'm not sure if I encountered Krstic on that same day or some other day, but I know I did encounter him because his command post was by the road that I had to take. So even if I had wanted to avoid him, I couldn't, and there was of course no reason why I would have wanted to avoid him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Sir, are you aware that when the OTP interviewed Zoran Malinic, that he informed them that he had no independent recollection of Mr. Beara being in Nova Kasaba on the 13th, if you're aware?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that. I don't know what Malinic told the Office of the Prosecutor of The Hague Tribunal. I know that nobody else but General Mladic was mentioned to me, when it came to senior officers. He was the only one who he mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Meek. Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, General.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I am Miodrag Stojanovic. Together with my colleagues, we represent Ljubomir Borovcanin and we respect your experience and your participation in the war, and I assume that throughout the war operations you participated in a number of combat activities, together with a special brigade of the police. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can we look at an exhibit together, which is 4D00120. This is a document that is part of the file under the title "Returning Lost Positions on Slivnjansko Brdo-Sokoline" in the period from the 1st of May, 1994, to the 21st of May, 1994. Just for the Chamber's information, these documents were located on the EDS as part of the collection from the Drina Corps. At this moment, Your Honours, we still don't have a translation, and since we will be using just one paragraph, I am kindly asking the Trial Chamber to allow me to have that paragraph interpreted in the courtroom. Can we look at the page number 3 of this analysis in B/C/S. Sir, can I kindly ask you to pay attention to the first paragraph on that page, page number 3, and if you could, for the sake of the interpreters, could you please read it aloud?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the beginning?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Just the first passage, starting with: "All forces ..."

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "All forces for active combat and for holding positions are resubordinated to the Command of the 2nd Romanija Motorised Brigade which were commanded by the commander of the 2nd Romanija Motorised Brigade, Colonel Krstic."

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to ask you this about this document: Do you remember that some of the troops of the special brigade of the police, under the command of Borovcanin [Realtime transcript read in error "Brdjanin"], participated in this combat operation? You can see this written in the fifth paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that, I remember it very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Will you agree with me, then, that you also participated in that operation, together with the other units that were present in that theatre of war?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'll agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have just been informed that on page 57, line 14, instead of "Unit under the command of Borovcanin," it says "Brdjanin." And I'll kindly ask for this to be corrected. I don't think that this should be a major problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: They have done it before.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Savcic, the objective of my analysis of this document is this, and it follows from this question: In such operations which involve a special brigade of the police or some of its troops, will you agree with me that these troops are resubordinated to the military unit in whose area of responsibility the operation is taking place?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. Who else they would receive their orders from? How else would they be able to perform any tasks if those tasks did not arrive from that particular unit?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Will we agree, then, that in other such operations in which you participated together with the brigade of the military police, the whole brigade or parts of the brigade were resubordinated to the military police unit in whose area of responsibility they were fighting?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I witnessed on many occasions, together with the -- with Mr. Borovcanin, starting with the end of 1992 to the end of the war in 1995, we had a number of occasions and situations that Protection Regiment and parts of the special brigade of the police were resubordinated to a certain higher command of the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I am waiting for the transcript. There is no other reason. Can we now look at a different document, which is 4D00725. This is an exhibit that we have already seen. This is the law on the implementation of the law on the interior affairs during war or under an imminent threat of war. Can we look at paragraph 14, which is on page 5 of the B/C/S. This is 4DP00725. The document number is 4DP00725. Can we look at page 5 in B/C/S or page 12 in English? While we are waiting for this to come up, let me just tell you that this is a law on the implementation of the law on the interior affairs during the state of war or imminent threat of war, and this was passed on the 29th of November, 1994, and that's -- and it came into effect on the 1st of December, 1994. Can we look at Article 14, paragraph 1 thereof, in which it is stated as follows: "Units of the police, which pursuant to an order of the supreme commander of the armed forces, are sent into combat, are resubordinated to the commander of the unit in whose area of responsibility they're supposed to carry out their combat orders." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Will we agree, then, that this is exactly what was confirmed by the answer that you provided to us previously and that your answer arises from this law?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is the law, and it cannot be interpreted in any other way. Way.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Can we look at the following document, which also confirms your answer. I would like to call up Exhibit number P00008 in the EDS system.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And while we are waiting for that, let me tell you, General, that it is an order issued by the supreme commander of the Armed Forces of Republika Srpska. The date is 22 April 1995. As you can see in the document, because of the problems and some ambiguities in the engagement of the MUP units in combat, elaborates on Article 14, I would kindly ask you to look at paragraph 1 in this document, in which it says: "The Main Staff of the army shall, in the future, provide more precise and a more concrete definition of the request to engage and use in combat of MUP units, in keeping with the provisions of Article 14 of the law on ..." that we have just mentioned. My question would be this: This order issued by the supreme commander of the armed forces dated the 22nd of April, 1995, does it also confirm what you've just told us, that you experienced in joint combat activities that involved the special brigade of the police?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I completely agree with you. I would even say -- give you an example that I sometimes had similar problems despite the fact that I was a member of the army. What does it mean to provide precision and clarification for the request? This means that members of the police wanted to know in advance what task they were being engaged in. For example, sometimes I would be sent to do some policing. I would take certain equipment and arms, and then my policing task would be transformed into a combat task and I would come unprepared. For that reason, there's probably a need, and the president of the Republic responded to the need and defined that in his order.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would kindly ask you to intervene when you deem necessary to stop for our next break. We -- the first time we had a break was at a time somewhat different than normally, so I would kindly ask and I'm entirely in your hands for our next break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I stand to be corrected, but I think the next break is due in about 32 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you wish to have a break now, Mr. Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am okay to continue. I don't have a problem with that. I just wanted to hear from you, when you wish your next break to be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The next break will be within 18 minutes, 18 minutes from now. All right? Quarter to. If anyone wishes a break now, we'll grant you a break now. I mean, it's -- because I see that there is some kind of conspiracy.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My impression is that my learned friend from the Prosecution would not mind a break now, so I was kind of ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. We'll have a 20 -- shall we reduce the break? We'll have a 25-minute break starting from now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: General, we left it off with the regulations regulating the issue of resubordination of the police to the Army of Republika Srpska, and with the fact that you participated in a lot of combat activities together with the special brigade of the police. My next question would be this: Will you agree with me that in all those combat operations in which you participated together with the special brigade of the police under the command of Mr. Ljubomir Borovcanin, and I'm referring to only those operations, you didn't have any problems executing the tasks that you received from the superior command?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will agree with you, there were no problems at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now I would like to show you a few more documents dealing with prisoners of war. You have already spoken about prisoners of war in your examination-in-chief, and in cross-examination you have mentioned prisoners of war who surrendered in the Nova Kasaba sector. Those prisoners of war were members of the 28th Division of the BiH Army. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You also spoke about these prisoners in your interview with Mr. McCloskey on the 17th October 2005, and just for those who following that, this is page 57 in B/C/S and 37 in English. On that occasion, you stated, amongst other things, that Zoran Malinic informed you that pursuant to an order by General Mladic, people from the football pitch in Nova Kasaba were handed over to the military police of the Bratunac Brigade in accordance with their territorial competence. This is what the transcript reads, and I'm asking you whether you remember that part of your interview with Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, I remember that, but I don't have the transcript in front of me at the moment. If I stated that they had been handed over to the military police of the Bratunac Brigade, then I misspoke. They were actually escorted from that football pitch. They got on the vehicles or buses, which were escorted by one or two soldiers in each of these vehicles. I don't know which unit they were from, and I wasn't interested in finding out.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Maybe this would be a good opportunity to dispel that dilemma, and may we look at 1D00196. 1D00196 is the number of the document. This is a transcript of your interview. I would kindly ask you to look at page 57 of B/C/S and page 37 in English. General, we will have the document on the screen in a minute. We shall look at it together, and then you can clarify that answer for us. Can we scroll down a little? Very well, thank you. I'm drawing your attention to page number 19 -- I apologise, line number 19 in the transcript, in which you stated as follows: "In Bratunac, they were handed over to the military police of the Bratunac Brigade, which means they respected their territorial competencies." Do you see that, General?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that, but I have to correct myself. Later on, we clarified my answer and we said that this was not in Bratunac but, rather, that from the football pitch, they were put onto buses and other vehicles. In other words, they were not escorted to Bratunac or to the Bratunac Brigade. I must have had wrong information. The prisoners of war were handed over in Bratunac, which made me conclude that they had escort to Bratunac. I apologise for this previously erroneous information that I provided.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, General. This was an attempt to clarify the answer, and the question that I would like to put to you is this: These prisoners of war, people who surrendered from the 28th Division, from the moment they were loaded onto the buses, were no longer under the protection and authority of your unit, you were no longer concerned with their safety, either personal or the safety of their property; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. At the moment they got on those buses, the 65th Protection Regiment no longer had anything to do with the prisoners of war, which means that we no longer had any responsibility for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: This is exactly the point of my question, and this is what I'm going to continue, I'm going to continue along these lines. You said earlier on that on one occasion you told Zoran Malinic that he had to abide by the military rules concerning prisoners of war. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And let's round this off. What do you mean by "abiding by the military rules concerning prisoners of war," what do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean their protection, an obligation on the part of the army to provide protection for their prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: May I continue? Tell me if I'm right or wrong. This applies for the duration of time when they are under your responsibility?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely so. That's the only time we can guarantee their safety, while they are our responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Let's see how this appears in various documents and regulations. Can we look at Exhibit number P00107, P00107? While we are waiting for the document to appear on the screen, let me just tell you that this is an order for active combat by the Command of the Drina Corps, and the title of the operation is [Realtime transcript read in error "Zvijezda-95"] Krivaja-95. The date on the document is 2nd July 1995. Can we please look at page 5 in B/C/S and page 7, lines 9 and 10, in English. Your Honours, there is a mistake in the transcript, page 65, line 7. The name of the operation is Krivaja-95, whereas in the transcript we read "Zvijezda-95."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: General, can we look at the fourth line from the top of the page in B/C/S, where it says: "The security organs and the military police will determine the sectors of collection and providing security for prisoners of war and war booty. The Geneva Conventions should be complied with in treating prisoners of war and the civilian population." Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can we agree that this is a schematic or a normal way to address subordinated units of the Corps Command when they embark on a combat operation, when it comes to the treatment of prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This passage that you've just read and that we see on the screen is part of the measures of combat support -- sorry, support to combat operations, namely, the part related to security. I wouldn't really agree that it is standard. Every particular mission requires particular measures of support, including security support. So it's not something that can automatically be applied to the next mission or any other mission. For every mission, in particular, measures of combat support have to be developed so that things would work in an optimal way and lead to success.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: That's precisely what I want to ask you through the next document, about this development. Could I have 4D0008, and that is an order of the Drina Corps dated 13 July 1995. Thank you. I think this is the document. Please look at point 3 in this order. Can we just scroll down a bit? So we are talking about the 13th, General. You will correct me if I'm wrong. This is a development of an elaboration on what you have just discussed, and it says: "The captured and disarmed Muslims are to be placed in adequate premises that can be secured with smaller forces, and immediately inform the superior command." Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Does this correspond, precisely to what you've just said, for every particular mission, every particular situation, an order has to be developed?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what practice dictates. It often happens that in a particular situation, things cannot work as was initially planned or the situation changes, like here, when the number of prisoners increased, and appropriate measures had to be taken to accommodate that. We had one situation when the -- at the planning stage, and now in the field things have to be adjusted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, for the record, line 11, I take it that the 65 ter number should be "4080," not "8."

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. We have noticed that already. We just waited for the witness to finish his answer. There is indeed a zero missing at the end of this number.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: General, shall we continue? So the question was: If one of the prisoners of war found themselves in the hands of parts of the military police units that were resubordinated then to the Drina Corps, do you agree with me that they, the special brigade of the police, would have to act in keeping with this order of the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please speak into the microphone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Now a question in principle. I believe we'll be able to agree. Prisoners of war are a logical consequence of every war. It's a natural development, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, most of the time. It often happens in fighting that one is captured and becomes a prisoner of war. It is nothing out of the ordinary in combat activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: So who is responsible in those circumstances in wartime, to take care of prisoners of war, their accommodation, providing food, treatment, et cetera, in principle?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the person or the entity who is responsible for the area in which the combat activities took place and where a certain number of prisoners of war were taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can we agree that in this specific case, if we are talking about the 13th, the Krivaja-95 operation, that would be the area of the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, the Drina Corps, but with this order that is still on the screen, the Drina Corps regulated that situation and issued specific instructions to its units on how to proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And to conclude this subject, this answer you just gave would also apply to the safety of the prisoners of war and preventing them from escaping? Your answer would be the same, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I have one more document to show you. Could we please take a look at 1D00197. We will have it on the screen in a moment, General. You will see that it is an article from June 1994, published in the "Policijac" publication, "Policemen," and it contains an interview with you. Could we scroll down a little and concentrate on the right-hand side?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For all intents and purposes, Witness, please note that since this extract from a newspaper contains a photo of yourself, we are not broadcasting it outside. Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please look at one paragraph? I'd like to look at it together with you. It reads -- in fact, you are saying this: "Saric, Borovcanin and I had this idea that we want to take the cooperation between the police and the army to the highest possible level. The special brigade of the police, units for special purposes of the police, have played a huge role in this war." Do you see this?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And I'll complete this. You go on to say: "The special brigade of the police has an extraordinary potential, well-trained and tested fighting men I think that is currently the best we have in Republika Srpska." Can you see this?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: This is just a cue for something I want to ask you. What is your personal and professional experience with Ljubomir Borovcanin as a commander in particular combat activities when he performed that activity instead of Saric? What do you think of him as a person, as a superior officer?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I first met Mr. Borovcanin in end 1992 when he was the commander of a public security station in Bratunac. We worked together on some cases of paramilitary organisation. We neutralised this evil that was starting to appear in the area of Republika Srpska, and our successful cooperation lasted throughout the war. I cannot now enumerate all the operations in which we worked together, but that cooperation turned into regular practice. Wherever we went, the commanders would assign us to be -- to work side by side, because they knew we had a good mutual relationship and understanding and that would contribute to overall success. I can also say that when one is choosing one's friends, one naturally chooses a person with many moral and human qualities and virtues. Ljubomir Borovcanin was always an example to his subordinates and to his colleagues, and at the height of battle he is a man who makes swift and right decisions which decide the outcome of the battle.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, General. I have no further question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Stojanovic. Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: General --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Petrusic, and today I'm going to have some questions to you on behalf of General Radivoje Miletic's Defence. Yesterday, on your examination-in-chief, you were stopped in mid-1995, in July 1995, when it came to your military career, and since you've said that you completed the highest military schools, including the General and Command Staff Academy, I'm interested in the period from July 1995 until the moment you retired. How did your career develop in the then Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yesterday when I spoke about my career, I didn't say anything about July 1995. I said that I was the commander of the Protection Regiment until January 1996. If I didn't say it yesterday, I'm saying it now. Then I was sent for education to the General Staff School of the then Army of Yugoslavia in Belgrade. Having completed that education, I was assigned to the duty of the assistant chief of the General Staff for Security. I stayed in that office until March 1998. Then I was placed at the disposal of the General Staff. I retired on the 30th of July, 2002.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: You had an occasion to familiarise yourself with the most important documents concerning the command of the army, of the prewar and postwar of the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: You talked about the organisation of the 65th Protection Regiment. You mentioned the Motorised Battalion that was deployed in the vicinity of Han Pijesak, or the way I understood it, it was in contact with the Zepa Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. I said at the beginning of my testimony that the Motorised Battalion did not keep its original shape. The need and the situation on the ground, it had to be incorporated into the establishment of the Protection Regiment. The Motorised Battalion that had been mobilised from the ranks of the local population, unlike the other units of the regiment which were made of conscripts, at the very beginning of the war this Motorised Battalion was on the strength of the 1st Romanija Brigade. Since the Command of the 1st Romanija Brigade was in Sarajevo, the Command was almost impossible. That's why it was incorporated into the 2nd Romanija Brigade. And then for the same reasons, the Main Staff decided that this Motorised Battalion which held positions facing the Zepa Brigade should become part of the Protection Regiment.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: In other words, that battalion was involved in constant conflicts, it came under constant attack by the terrorist groups which came out of Zepa and were moving towards the Main Staff; they were constantly in contact with them?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. The elements of the combat deployment of the battalion were always targeted. Those were not motorised companies, those were not major, big targets. They were rather the elements of logistics or the weaker elements. Unless they were protected and secure, elements were targeted most of the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: General, I would kindly ask you to make a short pause after my question. It is not my intention to establish who was it who started the conflict in the area, but we have heard witnesses here who claim that you are the -- the Army of Republika Srpska on the 14th of July, 1992, carried out an armed attack on the population of Zepa, on the town of Zepa. I have information that you were one of the participants in that event. I would kindly ask you to tell us what actually happened.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not participate in those events that you are asking me about. This happened on the 4th of June. On the following day, either on the 5th or on the 6th of June, I reported to the duty to which I had been assigned in Crna Rijeka. But since this went on after the 4th, I got involved in dealing with the problems that had arisen, and therefore I can say that as from the 5th or the 6th, I indeed did participate in those events. I must say that this was not an attack launched by the Army of Republika Srpska against Zepa, not at all. I have to say, Your Honours, that very often there was manipulation with the term "Zepa." Zepa was presented as a town, but the village of Zepa has no more than ten houses all together. Still, this doesn't matter when combat is taking place, but still we need to know the size of the place that is targeted. I was informed that the unit of the Republika Srpska Army had been given orders to move from Han Pijesak to the radio relay hub that is on the feature called "Zlovrh." In order to reach that feature, that feature held a permanent crew of the Army of Republika Srpska which maintained regular radio relay communication with the rest of the territory and the rest of the army. In order to be sure that there would be no misunderstanding, the local authorities, civilian and military authorities, got in touch with the representatives of the Muslim people, and they were explained that the movement of the Army Republika Srpska is aimed at carrying out a logistical task, and the logistical task was to provide the troops at Zlovrh with food, clothes and everything, all the other bare necessities. They were assured by Mr. Ramo Cader [phonetic] that there would be no problem, and this gentleman, I believe, was subsequently the chief of the Staff of the Zepa Brigade or, in any case, he had command position there. And this unit that was put together to carry out the task and consisted of the troops from the sector of Pale gave specific orders not to engage in any provocation which might be misinterpreted, in order to avoid any possible negative consequences. Having been given all these guarantees, they embarked on the execution of the task. They passed several Muslim villages, Stoborani, [indiscernible] and Brloznik, and between Brloznik and Borike villages, in a place that is very conducive to setting up ambushes, the column was attacked, and I believe that the Republika Srpska Army suffered the biggest losses ever in any one day. There were over 50 people killed. The rescue operation to pull out the dead and the wounded lasted for days, and that's the part in which I participated in. In other words, the Army of Republika Srpska was marching. It did not display combat deployment aimed at attacking a village or anything else in the territory populated by the Muslim population.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And do make sure, this was in 1992, not 1995, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are right, Mr. President. When I was putting my question, I said "the 4th of June," but I didn't mention the year.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Sir, as the Presiding Judge has just stated, the event took place on the 4th of June, 1992; am I right?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't pay much attention to the year. When you said "the 4th of June," I know it was in 1992, because in 1995 nothing happened on the 4th of June. And there's just one more thing that I would like to add. Within the Zepa Brigade, up to the end of the war, there existed a detachment called "The 4th of June." In other words, one unit within that brigade was named "The 4th of June" to commemorate the losses that they inflicted upon the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: After that, the Army of Republika Srpska did not retaliate, there was no operation staged against the Zepa Brigade or the armed population there, although at the time they existed as the 1st Zepa Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are right, there was nothing. The activity on the part of the Army of Republika Srpska concerning the Zepa territory and with the evacuation of the dead and wounded and some of the equipment, some equipment was left there in order to testify to that tragedy, and I believe that these things can still be found at the location. For example, one torched tank can still be seen there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Were there any other attacks on the part of the Muslims to the moment when the protected area was established?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, unfortunately, there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: In other words, we can say that when things are put in perspective, the notorious fact that after the establishment of the protected areas of Srebrenica and Zepa, in both enclaves the Muslims were duty-bound to surrender all their weapons, both their small arms as well as all other types of weaponry?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was the obligation, but they still continued with their combat activities, which proves that the obligation was not complied with.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: One might also say that the task of UNPROFOR, which had its observation points around both protected zones, and I'm currently talking about Zepa, was to take weapons away from any person or military establishment that they might find on the ground?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. UNPROFOR were supposed to carry out the militarisation and to take over or assume responsibility for the security of the protected area and the population in that protected area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, if at any time questions are put to which you would agree to stipulate, perhaps we can cut the testimony of this witness shorter. For example, this last question, I think you would have agreed without any reservations. So let's proceed, Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. You are correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My next question would call for my learned friend's agreement. I shall still put it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: We can then agree that UNPROFOR failed in their mission, because the establishment of the 28th Division proves that that mission failed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead. Answer the question, General.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've already said, in light of the combat activities from the area of protected areas, after their establishment, one can say that the UNPROFOR troops failed to carry out their mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in light of your remark, I am going to put a few more questions that are a well-known fact, and in the past the Prosecutor has never contested any of these facts, and I'm primarily talking about the attacks that were launched from the protected area of Zepa.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Petrusic, I hate to stop you, but if you're saying that the Prosecution has already agreed to these facts, why put them again to this witness in the first place? That's my first remark. The second thing: What's the relevance, all this, to what we should be talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that the Prosecutor has not shown the willingness to accept those facts as notorious, and, on the other hand, when it comes to the relevance in the indictment, it still says that military and paramilitary forces of the Army of Republika Srpska expelled the Muslim population from the territory of towns such as Vlasenica, Visegrad, Han Pijesak, into the area of Zepa.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Excuse me for entering into this at this point, but I've been here throughout, obviously, the whole trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thought you were leaving the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I will, if you would like me to. We have -- we're willing to stipulate that there were attacks outside the Zepa enclave and there was attacks outside the Srebrenica enclave, and that's aggravated the situation and played part of the role in why these attacks occurred. This is a long part of the history. I would even stipulate that UNPROFOR failed in their mission, and if you would stipulate that the VRS helped them fail. But aside from that, I don't know if that's helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's come to the essence of this gentleman's testimony, please, and to 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Bear with me for a moment, Your Honours, please. Could you please put on the screen P192 and at the same time, if it's possible, P35. I would also like to ask the usher to give the witness hard copies of these two exhibits, because I believe it might be easier for him to follow that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Petrusic, do you want them one after the other or juxtaposed?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If it's possible to split the screen, I would like to have them juxtaposed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think it may be possible, but I stand to be corrected. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: General, please look at the document on the left, issued by the Main Staff of the VRS on 13th July 1995, signed by the commander, General Ratko Mladic. This document is about preventing secret military information in the area of execution of combat activities from being divulged?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: It was addressed to your unit, among others. May I draw your attention to the seal as well, the stamp of receipt. What I can make out there, in this first line, it says it was received at 12.20.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, I see the same thing, 13th July at 1220 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: At any rate, it's much earlier than the time indicated on the document on the right numbered 192?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, at least one hour and 40 minutes earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Now, in the document on the right, the one that you do not claim you issued, there are certain assignments and recommendations as to how to perform certain tasks related to the prisoners of war; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I note that my learned friend has referred to the time that's indicated on the first line of the document on the bottom right-hand side of the page. I would ask that the witness also be instructed to look at the other times that are indicated on that same document. I'm not entirely sure that it's clear, from the question that was put to him or the answer, that he's had an opportunity to see that. In particular, I would direct his attention to the last line in the square, in the box that's on that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vanderpuye. Witness, you have heard that. Mr. Petrusic, would you proceed, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: General, would you agree that the contents of the order issued by the commander of the Main Staff, General Ratko Mladic, is basically the same as the contents of the proposal you sent to the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I look at the document on the left a bit more so that I can compare?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. While the witness is comparing, yes, Mr. Vanderpuye, you want to show him a hard copy?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If that is easier with you, Mr. Petrusic. I see Madam Fauveau nodding, so let's proceed that way. I can't see Mr. Petrusic. This is the problem. He's completely hidden behind the column, so I have to switch from video mode to e-court mode all the time to be able to follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I have also a hard copy of the other one which I could just hand to him, if it's easier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you agree to that, Ms. Fauveau and Mr. Petrusic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, let's compare them item by item. In the proposal of measures from the assistant commander for Intelligence and Security, the first point is to forbid access to all uninvited persons. And in the order of the commander of the Main Staff, we see basically the same, "Ban on access to the area of combat operations."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is going to take too long. I suppose you have compared them and contrasted them already. Could you just tell us where they differ instead of telling us where they are similar or identical?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, essentially, they are very similar. The third and the fourth points are a bit different. The third one deals with the battalion of the military police and its assignments, and in the order of the commander of the Main Staff the same paragraph relates to many more units, all units of the Drina Corps and two units attached to the Staff in some organs of the Main Staff. So they are similar, but the order of the commander of the Main Staff applies to a larger number of units and a larger area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: General, the Prosecutor suggested we look at the stamp again, so if I may ask the e-court directors to show us the box again. I don't know how qualified you are to answer this. It's a question better addressed to an encrypting officer, but if we move P35 to the right -- to the right. Right, that's it. You see the receipt stamp of the Romanija Motorised Brigade indicates the 14th of July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: So the time on the last line of this stamp -- could we move left again, to the left? Yes. On the last line, which says: "Transmitted 2230", and if we now go back to the very beginning, and you will see that this document was addressed to the Drina Corps, can you see that?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the Command of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And it reached the Command of the Drina Corps, which we know because the documentation from the Drina Corps and the rest was transmitted by the authorities of the Republika Srpska to the OTP, so I believe that the "2230" is the time when the Drina Corps sends this telegram to its subordinate unit, the Romanija Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really couldn't say anything about this stamp. It is the encryption men who are qualified. But it sounds logical, it makes sense that the other documents we have seen took the same path and took approximately the same time. And in this case, we have a document from the commander of the Main Staff which received probably greater priority than some other documents from lower levels.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we can stop here for the day. Mr. Petrusic, you will continue tomorrow, and then we will finish off also the remaining cross-examinations. General, we are stopping here. The same thing -- the same advise I gave you yesterday. You are not to communicate with anyone on the subject matter of your testimony. Have a nice evening, all of you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 13th day of September, 2007, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.00 p.m.,
